question: The implementation of co-funded educational programmes in Greece, especially within the framework of the ESF+ 2021-2027, raises serious issues regarding the effective use of European funds, respect for fundamental rights and equal access to education, especially for pupils with disabilities.

According to repeated reports, there are significant delays in the implementation of EUfunded programmes, shortages among teaching staff and support structures and a failure to provide the intended personalised support to pupils with disabilities.1 This situation leads to serious learning gaps, unequal treatment of pupils and the burden shifting to families.

The above may constitute a violation of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and the UNCRPD2, given that the European Structural Funds operate under shared management and national authorities bear the primary responsibility for the proper implementation of these programmes and are primarily responsible for ensuring their compliance with applicable EU regulations.3 In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the systematic problems in the implementation of cofinanced educational programmes in Greece, in particular as regards the support of pupils with disabilities?
In light of the above, how does the Commission assess Greece's compliance with its obligations under EU law, European financial rules and fundamental rights in the field of education?
What measures can the Commission take to ensure the full and substantive application of the rights of pupils with disabilities?

The school year began in September, however, the implementation of the co-financed programme ‘Remedial Teaching in Secondary Education, 2025-2026’ began with a three-month delay. As a result, a significant part of the planned remedial teaching has been lost, while, in many school units, Parallel Support for pupils with disabilities is not being provided as planned.

Often, the few teachers simultaneously cover pupils in large classes, without full coverage of teaching hours and without the necessary individualised support. See 20253rd Statistical Information Bulletin: Indicators for the access of children and people with disabilities to Education. Articles 14, 21, 24 and 26 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and Article 24 of the UNCRPD.

Given that these programmes are co-financed by European funds, questions arise as to their proper use, the effectiveness of national audit mechanisms and the responsibility of the competent authorities for ensuring compliance with EU law.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission monitors compliance with conditionalities1 within the Cohesion Policy programmes monitoring committees2.

The implementation of educational programmes cofinanced by the European Social Fund Plus3, including those supporting pupils with disabilities in Greece, are also monitored through regular reporting mechanisms, audits and meetings with national authorities.

Issues like delays in programme execution, staff shortages or needs for personalised support are assessed to ensure that the rights of people with disabilities are promoted and protected, while considering Member States' shared management responsibilities for effective and inclusive programme delivery.

The Commission recalls that under shared management the national authorities are responsible for ensuring compliance with applicable EU law, including with fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union4 throughout the implementation of EU-funded projects.

The enhanced Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities up to 20305 further promotes independent living and accessible educational environments for the full inclusion of persons with disabilities in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities to which the EU and all Member States are parties6.

In line with the division of competences in the area of education set out in Article 165 of Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union7, the Commission promotes inclusive education under the European Education Area by fostering mutual learning opportunities, providing policy guidance to Member States, supporting progress towards EU-level targets, and offering funding via Erasmus+ and Cohesion policy funds, with the aim of advancing inclusive practices.

1 Accessibility is also a horizontal principle in the design and implementation of Cohesion policy funds support. 2 The Commission monitors closely the programmes’ implementation in line with the EU regulation and

programme priorities. 3 https://european-social-fund-plus.ec.europa.eu/en; https://european-social-fund-plus.ec.europa.eu/en/supportyour-country/esf-greece. 4 https://fra.europa.eu/en/eu-charter. 5 Enhancing the Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities up to 2030 https://commission.europa.
